# Implement block: Bento Expand Grid (SwiftUI)

You are adding the "Bento Expand Grid" block from Native Cook to the user's iOS app. The block already exists as working SwiftUI code. Your job is to bring it into this project faithfully, not to write a new one that looks similar.

## The block

A bento of seven field notes on warm paper under a serif "Slow crafts" title: a tall photo of a desk, a near-black tile with "1,284 pages" read this season, a photo of tea being poured, a little map of a riverside walk drawn in thin lines with a dashed route and an orange pin, a wide quote tile ("The hands remember what the mind forgets."), a tall photo of clay-covered hands and a wide photo of a reading room. Tapping a tile grows it in place into its own page while the other tiles are pushed away and fade, nearest first: the photo, map or number becomes the page's header and a paper sheet slides up over it with a kicker, a serif title, a byline, a lead, a pull quote with an orange rule and two photos side by side. Scrolling slides the sheet over the header, which drifts up more slowly; dragging the page down from the top shrinks it into a floating card under the finger, and letting go puts it back in its tile.

**Motion.** The grid is four columns by four rows inside 16 pt margins with 10 pt gaps; tiles have 22 pt rounded corners and press to 97% in 120 ms. The open page is one clipped frame that moves between the tile and the screen on a spring (duration 800 ms, damping ratio 0.88) with a light haptic, its corners closing to 0; it lifts on a soft shadow while it flies. Its face fills the whole frame for the first 20% of the way and gives way to a header 48% of the screen tall by 80%, the sheet sliding up under it with a 28 pt overlap; the sheet's paper comes in between 22% and 42%, and its five blocks rise 18 pt as they fade in, from 42% of the way, each 6% later and taking 30%. Photos are drawn with cover cropping at every size, so the tile's crop grows into the header's; the map is redrawn at each size with lines of constant width; the stat and quote are set at up to 1.75 times their tile and scaled down into it, so their type stays sharp, and they grow anchored at the header's foot. The other tiles are pushed 44 pt straight away from the open one, shrink by 10% and fade, nearest first, each 0.07 later. The header slides up at 45% of the scroll. Dragging down from the top of the page (not while scrolled) shrinks it by up to 34% over half the screen, following the finger 60% across and 75% down and rounding its corners to 36 pt, while the grid comes back in behind it, up to 80% over the first quarter of the screen; a release past 110 pt or faster than 800 pt/s closes it into its tile on a spring (680 ms, 0.9) carrying the finger's speed, anything else springs back (420 ms, 0.82). The close button closes it the same way. The self-playing demo loops every 14 s: the desk opens at 1 s, its page scrolls 240 pt at 2.3 s over 1.1 s on an ease-in-out curve (0.77, 0, 0.175, 1) and back at 3.9 s over 0.8 s, is dragged down 150 pt at 5 s and closes at 5.5 s; the reading stat opens at 7.1 s, scrolls at 8.5 s and back at 10 s, closes from its button at 11 s, and the grid rests until the loop starts over. A touch stops the demo for 3 s, 7 s while a page is open, after which an open page closes and the loop starts over. Under reduced motion the page cross-fades in and out over 220 ms at full screen, nothing is pushed or scaled, the header does not drift, a drag down only closes it on release, and the demo does not play. Header photos are fetched at 1200 px (the tile shares the same copy) and the photos inside the page at 600 px, ahead of time.

## Reference source

The block is built and running in the Native Cook source repository. Each link below is a file on GitHub. To read one as plain text, replace `https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/` with `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/` in its address.

### Demo (start here)

- [BentoExpandGridDemo.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Cards/BentoExpandGrid/BentoExpandGridDemo.swift)

### Files of the block

- [BentoExpandGrid.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Cards/BentoExpandGrid/BentoExpandGrid.swift)
- [BentoExpandGridEngine.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Cards/BentoExpandGrid/BentoExpandGridEngine.swift)
- [BentoExpandGridMotion.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Cards/BentoExpandGrid/BentoExpandGridMotion.swift)
- [BentoExpandGridNotes.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Cards/BentoExpandGrid/BentoExpandGridNotes.swift)

### Frameworks

It needs no framework beyond SwiftUI.

## Your instructions

_Anything specific to this app goes here: where the block should appear, what to rename, what to change. Left empty, integrate the block as it is._

## How to work

Work like an experienced iOS engineer joining an existing project: learn the app first, read only what you need, decide early how the block fits, then integrate it with as little disruption as possible. Take the steps in order.

**Done means** the block is reachable in the user's app and behaves like the reference in the iOS Simulator or on a device. A SwiftUI preview is useful while you work, but it is not the proof: build and run the app.

**Fidelity.** Bring over the real implementation. Keep its structure, colours, sizes, timings and curves. Change only what this project requires and what "Your instructions" ask for.

If you already learned this project earlier in the conversation, reuse what you know and skip step 2. Learn it again only if the project changed or something you need is missing.

### 1. Check where you are

- You need the project's files and a terminal. If this prompt was pasted into a chat that has neither, stop and say so: it has to be run by a coding agent opened on the project.
- Confirm the project is an iOS app built with Xcode (an `.xcodeproj`, an `.xcworkspace` or a Swift package with an app target). If it is something else, stop, say what you found, and do not create a new app inside it unless the instructions ask for one.

### 2. Learn the host app

- The app target, its deployment target and its Swift version.
- SwiftUI, UIKit or both, and how a screen is shown today: `NavigationStack`, a coordinator, a tab bar, a storyboard.
- How files join the target: a folder the project synchronises, or a file list in the project that you have to extend.
- Conventions: folder layout, naming, where colours, fonts and assets live.
- Type names the app already uses, so the block's types do not collide with them.

### 3. Read the block

- Swift files in a module do not import each other, so the demo alone will not lead you to the rest. The list above names every file of the block: read them all.
- The demo is how the source repository shows the block. Bring over what the demo shows, not the repository's gallery. Anything listed under "Used by the demo only" stays behind.
- Read the block's initialiser and its defaults. The demo may switch on an option that makes the block play by itself for a recording (for example `autoPlay`). Keep the option; leave it off in the user's app unless asked.

### 4. Decide the fit

- The source app targets iOS 17. If the host targets an older system, check each API the block uses and tell the user what would have to change before you lower anything. Do not raise the host's deployment target without asking.
- If a type or function name of the block already exists in the app, rename the block's one, in every file that uses it, and say that you did.
- Shared helpers: copy the ones the block uses next to it, or fold them into the block's files. Do not copy helpers it never calls.
- In a UIKit app, show the block through a `UIHostingController`.

### 5. Bring it in

- Add the block's files to the app target, keeping their names.
- Copy its asset catalogs, loose resources and fonts, and check that the names the code asks for match the names in the bundle: a wrong name compiles and then shows nothing.
- A `.metal` file has to be compiled into the same target as the code that calls its function.
- Keep reduced-motion handling, haptics and accessibility labels as they are in the source.
- Mount the block where the instructions say. With no instructions, add a screen named after the block and make it reachable the way the app's other screens are.

### 6. Run it

- Build the app target for a simulator with `xcodebuild` or the project's own script, and fix every error and new warning the block introduced.
- Run it and use the block: every state, every gesture, light and dark appearance if the block follows them, and once with Reduce Motion on.
- If the build or the simulator fails for a reason outside the block, report the error and ask how to continue.

### 7. Report

- Files added and changed, and anything renamed to avoid a collision.
- How to reach the block in the app.
- Anything that differs from the reference, and why.
